title: Javascript ES6 Spread Operator
summary: Introduces the ES6 spread operator (...) for arrays and objects, then uses it together with computed property names to collapse the long if/else state updater from the previous challenge into a few lines.

concepts.heading: Spread with arrays
points: `...arr` written inside an array literal expands the array into its individual elements at that position. It replaces looping and pushing each item.
Position matters: `[...citrus, "Apple"]` puts the citrus items first, `["Apple", ...citrus, "Banana"]` inserts them between Apple and Banana, and putting it last appends them.
The spread creates a new array; the source array is not modified.
Demo: citrus = Lime, Lemon, Orange spread into a fruits array of Apple, Banana, Coconut; logging fruits shows a single flat array.

concepts.heading: Spread with objects
points: `...obj` inside an object literal copies all of that object's key-value pairs into the new object, alongside any other properties written next to it.
Example: spreading a fullName object (fName, lName) into a user object with id and username yields one flat object with four keys.
Contrast with listing the object by name (`{ fullName, id }`): that nests it under a `fullName` key instead of merging its keys.
(Extra) If the same key appears twice, the later one wins, so put overrides after the spread. This is why the state updater puts the new field last.
(Extra) The spread is shallow: nested objects are copied by reference.

concepts.heading: Applying it to the handleChange updater
points: All the if/else-if branches can be deleted. Return a new object that spreads the previous state and then adds the changed field.
Everything unchanged is carried over by `...prevValue`; the single trailing key-value pair overwrites just the field that changed.

First attempt `{ ...prevValue, name: value }` does not work: JavaScript treats `name` as the literal key "name", so state gains an unwanted `name` property and the real field never updates. The destructured `name` variable is flagged as unused.
Using `event.target.name` as the key also fails, since any text before the colon in an object literal is read as a string key, not an expression.

Fix: wrap the key in square brackets, `[name]: value`. This computed property name syntax evaluates the expression and uses its result as the key. Before ES6 the equivalent was creating an empty object and assigning `obj[key] = value`.
It is available here because Babel (via React's tooling) handles modern syntax.

concepts.heading: Going shorter, and why not to
points: With only one returned object the `return` and outer braces can be dropped, but the object literal must be wrapped in parentheses: `(prev) => ({ ...prev, [name]: value })`. Otherwise the braces are parsed as a function body.

That makes the updater two lines, but the instructor prefers the explicit return version because stacked braces and parentheses are harder to read. Rule: shorten code only while the meaning stays clear.
Practice recommendation: experiment with it before the next challenge.

pitfalls: Writing `name: value` instead of `[name]: value` creates a literal key called name.
Forgetting parentheses around an object returned from an arrow function with an implicit return.
Placing the spread after the new field, which makes the old value overwrite the new one.
(Extra) Spread copies are shallow, so nested objects still share references.

Tasks: (1) build a combined fruits array with spread at different positions, (2) merge two objects into one flat object, (3) show the nested-versus-flat difference, (4) fix a broken `{...prev, name: value}` updater, (5) rewrite a long if/else updater with spread.
